title: Tenali and the Mango Thief (Español)

full_text:
In King Krishnadevaraya’s private botanical garden grew a solitary Alphonso mango tree, renowned for producing the sweetest, most fragrant golden mangoes in South India.
As the prized fruits began to ripen, someone began stealing two ripe mangoes every night, climbing over the high palace garden walls.
The captain of the royal guard posted extra sentries, but the thief managed to slip through the dense foliage undetected.

The King was annoyed and summoned Tenali Raman:
'Tenali, if my own private garden cannot be guarded, how shall I defend an empire? Find the thief within twenty-four hours!'

Tenali inspected the mango tree.
He noticed that the tree’s lower trunk was smooth and required a climber to wrap both arms and thighs tightly around the bark to shinny up into the branches.

Tenali went to the palace apiary and procured two large earthenware jars of thick, sticky, dark forest honey.
At dusk, Tenali thoroughly smeared the entire lower six feet of the mango tree trunk with the thick, sticky honey, mixed with a fine powder of yellow ochre dye that left an indelible yellow stain on cloth.

The next morning, three ripe mangoes were missing.
Tenali smiled and said to the King:
'Maharaj, summon all fifty palace gardeners, guards, and kitchen assistants to the courtyard for the morning inspection.'

When the men assembled in neat ranks, Tenali walked along the rows, holding a large, buzzing jar of honeybees.
As Tenali walked past the third row of guards, a swarm of bees from the garden flew straight toward a guard named Mallesh!
The bees buzzed excitedly around Mallesh’s thighs and palms!

Mallesh was visibly squirming, trying desperately to keep his hands flat against his sides.
Tenali stepped forward and commanded:
'Mallesh, show your palms and raise your dhoti!'

Mallesh’s palms were completely coated in sticky honey and yellow dye, and the inner fabric of his trousers was soaked with honey and yellow tree bark marks!
He had shinnied up the sticky trunk in the dark, stolen the mangoes, and was unable to wash away the thick honey before morning inspection!

Caught in the sweet trap, Mallesh fell to the ground, confessed his thefts, and returned the stolen fruit.
The King was delighted by Tenali’s ingenious botanical trap:
'Tenali, thou hast caught the thief using nature’s own sweetness!'
Mallesh was reassigned to the cactus clearing division, and the royal mangoes remained safe.
moral: A thief cannot wash away the sticky consequences of his own crime. [ES]
